raw_case_text:
A 31-year-old man was referred to us for a symptomatology of 2-week duration. Past medical history was unremarkable. The patient reported unprotected receptive oral sex one month earlier with a male whose status for HIV was unknown. The patient complained from abdominal pain, arthralgia of ankles and wrists, and purpura of legs.
On examination, an extensive vascular purpura of the legs was present without other abnormalities. Biopsy of the skin revealed signs of vasculitis. Standard biological exams were normal, except for a mild proteinuria (0.5 g/L). Creatinemia was normal (0.9 mg/dL). Complement was normal. Anti-DNA antibodies were negative. A mixed cryoglobulinemia was detected in the serum. HCV and HBV serology were negative. HCV serology was done one year later and remained negative.
HIV testing was positive on ELISA while an incomplete profile was found on western blot (gp120 +/-, gp41++++, p31-, p24+). p24 antigenemia was positive (28 pg/mL). HIV viral load (VL) was 4.7 log copies/mL. CD4 cells count was 213/mm3. Antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir, emtricitabine, and r/atazanavir) was given. After 3 months of treatment, VL was <50 copies/mL and CD4 cells count was 924/mm3. Western blot was repeated and was subsequently positive for all bands tested. During this period, symptoms progressively decreased with a complete resolution after 3 months. Cryoglobulinemia became negative after 1 year of treatment. After a followup of 3 years, the patient remained asymptomatic with CD4 cells count always above 500/mm3 and VL <50 copies/mL.
Prevalence of cryoglobulinemia is high in HIV-infected patients. Scotto et al. found a prevalence of 6% for HIV-monoinfected patients and 14.2% for HIV-HCV-coinfected patients. In spite of this high prevalence, cryoglobulinemia is rarely symptomatic even if rare neurological, dermatological, renal, or rheumatological complications have been described. These complications occurred usually during chronic phase of HIV infection. To our knowledge, it has been not reported during acute primary infection. At presentation, our patient clearly suffered from symptomatic cryoglobulinemia. Clinical and anatomopathological findings were consistent with this hypothesis ruling out an incidental discovery of a cryoglobulinemia during HIV infection. The simultaneous occurrence of symptomatic cryoglobulinemia and HIV primary infection argued in favour of a role of HIV in the appearance of cryoglobulinemia. The impact of HAART on disappearance of cryoglobulinemia in our observation is difficult to establish.
Nevertheless, we cannot rule out a positive effect given that, in epidemiologic studies, prevalence of cryoglobulinemia in HIV-infected patients has decreased in HAART era.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old male presenting with a 2-week history of abdominal pain, ankle and wrist arthralgias, and purpura of the lower extremities.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed diffuse abdominal pain, bilateral ankle and wrist arthralgias, and extensive lower extremity purpura over a 2-week period. He reported an episode of unprotected receptive oral sex one month prior with a male partner of unknown health status.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history; no prior hospitalizations, chronic medical conditions, or drug allergies. Epidemiological history: unprotected receptive oral intercourse with a male partner of unknown health status one month prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for abdominal pain, bilateral wrist and ankle arthralgia, and cutaneous purpura; negative for macroscopic hematuria, fever, night sweats, or unintentional weight loss. Home medications: none. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Extensive palpable vascular purpura on both lower extremities without other cutaneous or systemic physical examination abnormalities. Vital signs normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum creatinine: 0.9 mg/dL; urinalysis: mild proteinuria (0.5 g/L); serum complement: normal; anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) autoantibodies: negative; viral hepatitis serologies: HBV and HCV serologies negative (repeat HCV serology negative at 1 year). Serum mixed cryoglobulinemia: detected.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin punch biopsy: histopathologic signs of leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Symptomatic mixed cryoglobulinemic leukocytoclastic vasculitis secondary to acute primary human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) infection. Autoimmune vasculitides ruled out by normal complement and negative anti-dsDNA; chronic viral hepatitis B and C ruled out by repeatedly negative serologies. HIV-1 confirmation: ELISA positive with evolving Western blot pattern (gp120+/-, gp41++++, p31-, p24+), positive p24 antigenemia (28 pg/mL), plasma HIV RNA viral load 4.7 log10 copies/mL, and CD4 cell count 213/mm3. Management & Outcome: Initiated on combination antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir, emtricitabine, and ritonavir-boosted atazanavir). Symptoms progressively subsided with complete clinical resolution within 3 months, accompanied by viral suppression (<50 copies/mL), CD4 count rising to 924/mm3, complete Western blot seroconversion, and disappearance of serum cryoglobulinemia at 1 year, maintaining clinical and virological remission at 3-year follow-up.
